stem: A company runs an app on EC2 and a database on Amazon RDS. An auditor asks who is responsible for OS patching in each case and for security group rules. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: AWS patches the EC2 guest OS on request; the customer patches the RDS database engine
Customer: EC2 guest OS and all SGs; AWS: the RDS operating system
AWS patches both guest operating systems
The customer patches both guest operating systems; AWS manages the security groups

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With EC2 (IaaS) the customer owns everything from the guest OS up: patches, software, and security group rules. With RDS, a managed service, AWS patches the underlying OS and database engine (in maintenance windows), but network access controls such as security groups remain the customer's responsibility.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS patching the EC2 guest OS: EC2 is customer-managed from the OS up.
• Customer patching RDS's OS: customers have no OS access on RDS; AWS handles it.
• 'On request' patching: there is no such model. Customers can use Systems Manager Patch Manager themselves.

Key takeaway: responsibility shifts toward AWS as services become more managed, but configuration of access (SGs, IAM, encryption choices) always stays with the customer.

stem: An attacker phished the root user's password for a company account, but the login attempt failed. Which control MOST likely stopped it, and what else should be done with the root user?

choices.text: An IAM password policy; also share the root password only with two administrators
MFA on root; also delete root access keys
An SCP denying all root actions in the management account; also enable CloudTrail
A permissions boundary on the root user; also rotate its access keys monthly

explanation:
Why this is correct:
MFA requires a second factor beyond the password, so a stolen password alone can't sign in. Best practice is also to delete root access keys and reserve the root user for the few tasks only it can perform.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Permissions boundaries: can't be applied to the root user.
• SCPs: don't apply to the management account, and they don't stop sign-in.
• Password policy: applies to IAM users, not root, and sharing the root password increases risk.

Key takeaway: protect root with MFA, no access keys, and minimal use.

stem: A company has 12 AWS accounts and wants employees to sign in once using their existing corporate Active Directory credentials and then access any of the accounts they are authorized for, without creating separate IAM users in each account. Which solution meets this requirement with the least ongoing administrative overhead?

choices.text: A bastion host that stores credentials for each of the 12 accounts
IAM Identity Center connected via AD Connector
An IAM user in every account for each employee, synced by script
A shared IAM user whose access keys are distributed to the team

explanation:
Why this is correct:
IAM Identity Center with AD Connector lets employees use corporate AD credentials for single sign-on to all 12 accounts, with permission sets per account.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bastion storing credentials: insecure and not SSO.
• Synced IAM users: long-term credentials and sprawl.
• Shared IAM user: no accountability.

Key takeaway: workforce SSO across accounts → Identity Center.

stem: A security team wants to permanently prevent any IAM principal in a set of member accounts, including account administrators, from disabling AWS CloudTrail, even if their IAM policies would otherwise allow it. Which approach achieves this?

choices.text: A deny statement added to each user's identity-based policy in every account
An IAM permissions boundary attached to every user and role in the accounts
An SCP denying CloudTrail stop and delete actions
Amazon GuardDuty enabled to detect CloudTrail tampering in each account

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An SCP that denies cloudtrail:StopLogging and DeleteTrail applies to every principal in member accounts, including administrators and the root user, and they can't remove it themselves.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Deny in each user's policy: admins can edit it.
• Permissions boundaries: per principal and editable by admins.
• GuardDuty: detects, doesn't prevent.

Key takeaway: guardrails admins can't bypass → SCPs.

stem: A development team is deploying an application on EC2 instances that needs to call other AWS services such as S3 and DynamoDB. Which approach is the AWS-recommended way to grant this access?

choices.text: Attach an IAM role to the EC2 instance profile
Store an IAM user's access key and secret key in the application's configuration file
Hardcode the credentials in the application source code
Use the AWS account's root credentials

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An IAM role attached through an instance profile provides automatically rotated temporary credentials, with no keys stored in the application.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Access keys in config: long-term secrets.
• Hardcoded credentials: worst practice.
• Root credentials: never.

Key takeaway: EC2 → AWS APIs = instance profile role.

stem: A company wants its web tier to survive a data center power failure and also a natural disaster affecting an entire metropolitan area. Latency between web servers and the database must stay low. Which design fits?

choices.text: Instances spread across edge locations, with the database in one Availability Zone
Instances across two Regions, replicating synchronously
Instances across multiple AZs in one Region, plus a DR copy in another Region
Instances in one AZ across racks, plus multiple Local Zones for disaster recovery

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AZs are isolated from one another (separate power and facilities) but connected with low latency, so a multi-AZ deployment survives a facility failure while keeping database latency low. A Region-wide disaster needs a copy in another Region.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Racks and Local Zones: a single AZ fails as a unit, and Local Zones are extensions of a parent Region, not a DR design.
• Edge locations: serve CloudFront and Route 53, not EC2 web tiers.
• Synchronous cross-Region replication: adds high latency to every write.

Key takeaway: AZs are for high availability; Regions are for disaster recovery.

stem: A company runs Microsoft Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS) on-premises and wants employees to access the AWS Management Console using their existing corporate credentials, without deploying AWS Directory Service. Which mechanism enables this?

choices.text: AWS Direct Connect between the corporate network and AWS
A NAT gateway between the corporate network and the VPC
SAML 2.0 federation with AD FS and IAM roles
IAM users kept in sync with the same passwords as AD accounts

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SAML 2.0 federation with AD FS maps AD groups to IAM roles, so employees sign in to the console with corporate credentials.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Direct Connect: networking, not identity.
• NAT gateway: networking.
• Synced IAM users: duplicates identities.

Key takeaway: existing SAML IdP → federation to IAM roles.

stem: A role in Account B must read objects in a bucket in Account A. The role's identity policy allows s3:GetObject on the bucket, but access is denied. The objects use SSE-S3. What is missing?

choices.text: An SCP in Account A that explicitly allows access from Account B
A permissions boundary in Account B that also lists s3:GetObject
A bucket policy in Account A granting the role access
A KMS key policy granting Account B decrypt permissions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cross-account access needs permission on both sides: the identity policy in B (already present) and a resource-based policy in A (the bucket policy) that trusts B's principal. Only resource-based policies can grant access to principals in other accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Permissions boundary: only limits permissions; it never grants access.
• SCPs: never grant permissions; they only restrict.
• KMS key policy: SSE-S3 uses S3-managed keys, so no KMS policy is involved.

Key takeaway: cross-account = identity policy on the caller side + resource policy on the owner side.

stem: Team A in Account 111111111111 needs to grant Team B in Account 222222222222 read-only access to objects in an S3 bucket owned by Account A, without creating any IAM users in Account A. Which solution is most appropriate?

choices.text: A bucket policy granting s3:GetObject to Account B's principal
Email the bucket owner's access keys to Team B securely
A NAT gateway shared between both accounts' VPCs
Public read access on the bucket, limited by object prefix

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A bucket policy in Account A granting s3:GetObject to Account B's principal (plus B's IAM permission) allows cross-account read access.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Emailing keys: insecure.
• NAT gateway: networking, not authorization.
• Public read: exposes data.

Key takeaway: cross-account S3 → bucket policy + IAM.

stem: An organization needs a control that sets the maximum permissions for every IAM principal across dozens of member accounts, while a separate team also wants to cap what a specific IAM role can do within one account even if its identity-based policy is broader. Which pairing of controls fits these two requirements respectively?

choices.text: A permissions boundary organization-wide and an SCP for the single role
Two permissions boundaries attached to the Organizations root
SCP organization-wide; permissions boundary for the role
Two SCPs, one nested inside the other at different OUs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SCPs set the maximum permissions across member accounts. A permissions boundary caps a single role's permissions within an account.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Boundary org-wide: boundaries attach to principals, not organizations.
• Boundaries on the root: not possible.
• Nested SCPs: can't target one role.

Key takeaway: org ceiling → SCP; single principal ceiling → permissions boundary.

stem: A company wants to deny all IAM users the ability to delete S3 buckets unless they have authenticated with MFA. Which IAM policy element should be used to enforce this?

choices.text: An SCP that blocks the S3 service for users without MFA devices
A resource policy on IAM that requires MFA for bucket actions
A permissions boundary that lists s3:DeleteBucket as not allowed
A Deny when aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is false

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Deny statement for s3:DeleteBucket with the condition aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent false (BoolIfExists) blocks deletion unless the user authenticated with MFA.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SCP blocking S3 entirely: too broad.
• Resource policy on IAM: doesn't exist.
• Boundary listing not allowed: boundaries don't use deny lists this way.

Key takeaway: require MFA for sensitive actions → Deny with MFA condition.

stem: A mobile app, a CI system in another cloud, and EC2 instances all need AWS access without storing long-term keys. Which service issues the credentials they would use?

choices.text: AWS STS, issuing temporary credentials via AssumeRole and web-identity APIs
AWS KMS, issuing data keys that authorize API calls for a limited time
IAM, generating new access keys for each session and deleting them afterward
AWS Secrets Manager, rotating a shared IAM user key every hour

explanation:
Why this is correct:
STS issues temporary credentials: instance profiles use it for EC2, AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity for OIDC-based workloads like external CI or mobile identity providers, and AssumeRole for cross-account access. They expire automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• KMS data keys: encrypt data; they aren't API credentials.
• Per-session IAM keys: still long-term keys, and churning them is error-prone.
• Rotating a shared user key: still long-term credentials shared across workloads.

Key takeaway: no long-term keys → STS temporary credentials behind roles.

stem: A company is setting up a multi-account AWS environment from scratch and wants a pre-built landing zone with baseline security guardrails, automated account provisioning, and centralized logging across accounts. Which service should they use?

choices.text: Amazon Inspector
AWS Control Tower
AWS Trusted Advisor
AWS Config alone

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Control Tower sets up a landing zone with baseline accounts, guardrails, and centralized logging.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Inspector: vulnerabilities.
• Trusted Advisor: recommendations.
• Config alone: compliance rules without a landing zone.

Key takeaway: multi-account baseline → Control Tower.

stem: What is a key difference between an IAM group and an IAM role?

choices.text: IAM groups and roles are identical except for how they are named in the console
IAM roles can only be assumed by the root user of the account
A group bundles users with shared policies; a role is assumed for temporary credentials
An IAM group can be assumed by an EC2 instance, while a role cannot be

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A group is a collection of users that share attached policies. A role is an identity that trusted principals assume to get temporary credentials.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Identical: they differ.
• Only root assumes roles: any trusted principal can.
• Groups assumed by EC2: groups can't be assumed.

Key takeaway: groups organize users; roles are assumed.

stem: A developer with an IAM policy that grants s3:PutObject on a bucket reports getting Access Denied errors when uploading, even though no changes were made to their IAM policy. The member account belongs to an AWS Organization. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The S3 bucket's storage class does not support PutObject operations
An SCP explicitly denies s3:PutObject, overriding the IAM allow
The developer's console password has expired, blocking API calls
The bucket is in a different Availability Zone from the developer

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An SCP explicit deny overrides any IAM allow. If uploads fail despite IAM permission, check SCPs (and bucket policies).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Storage class: doesn't block PutObject.
• Expired console password: doesn't affect API keys.
• Different AZ: buckets aren't in AZs.

Key takeaway: explicit deny anywhere wins.

stem: A developer role currently has s3:* on all buckets because 'it's easier'. The team needs the role to upload only to one prefix in one bucket. Which change best applies least privilege, and how can the team find what's actually used?

choices.text: Keep s3:* but add a permissions boundary that allows s3:* on all buckets
Keep s3:* and rely on CloudTrail
Scope to PutObject on the prefix; verify with Access Analyzer
Replace s3:* with AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess, since reading is safer than writing

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Least privilege means granting only the actions and resources needed: PutObject on arn:aws:s3:::bucket/prefix/*. Access Analyzer can generate a policy from CloudTrail activity, showing which actions were actually used.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Boundary allowing s3:*: doesn't narrow anything.
• Read-only access: removes the needed write permission and still grants reads everywhere.
• CloudTrail only: detection after misuse, not prevention.

Key takeaway: scope both actions and resources, and use usage data to trim.

stem: A web server in a public subnet accepts HTTPS. The security group allows inbound 443, and the NACL allows inbound 443 and outbound 443. Clients time out. What is wrong?

choices.text: The stateful security group needs an outbound rule for ephemeral response ports
The NACL needs an inbound ephemeral rule, since replies arrive on ephemeral ports
Security groups are evaluated before NACLs, so the NACL rules are ignored
The NACL must allow outbound ephemeral ports for replies

explanation:
Why this is correct:
NACLs are stateless: responses to clients go out to the client's ephemeral port, so outbound rules must allow that range. Security groups are stateful and allow return traffic automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SG outbound rule for replies: SGs track connections, so return traffic is already allowed.
• Inbound ephemeral: the replies leave the server; inbound ephemeral matters for connections the server initiates.
• Evaluation order: both layers apply; neither is skipped.

Key takeaway: stateless NACLs need rules in both directions, including ephemeral ports.

stem: A company wants its backend database servers to have outbound internet access for software updates but must not be directly reachable from the internet. Which architecture achieves this?

choices.text: Assign public IP addresses to the database servers and restrict inbound ports
Remove the security groups from the database servers to allow updates
Place the database servers in a public subnet with an internet gateway
Private subnet with outbound routing via a NAT gateway

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Servers in a private subnet with a 0.0.0.0/0 route to a NAT gateway get outbound internet access but no inbound path.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public IPs: expose the servers.
• Removing security groups: insecure (and not possible).
• Public subnet: directly reachable.

Key takeaway: outbound-only internet → private subnet + NAT.

stem: A public API behind CloudFront and an ALB is regularly hit by large DDoS attacks. The company wants 24/7 help from AWS DDoS experts during attacks and credits for scaling charges caused by attacks. What should it enable?

choices.text: AWS Shield Advanced on the CloudFront distribution and ALB
AWS WAF rate-based rules alone on the distribution
Amazon GuardDuty with automated blocking of attacking IPs
AWS Shield Standard, which is included and covers these needs automatically

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Shield Advanced adds enhanced detection and mitigation, access to the Shield Response Team, and DDoS cost protection for scaling charges on protected resources.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shield Standard: automatic L3/L4 protection for everyone, but no response team or cost protection.
• WAF rate rules alone: help with HTTP floods, but no expert support or cost protection.
• GuardDuty: threat detection for accounts and workloads, not DDoS mitigation.

Key takeaway: expert DDoS support + cost protection → Shield Advanced.

stem: A security team wants continuous, automated threat detection across their AWS accounts that analyzes VPC flow logs, DNS logs, and CloudTrail events to identify potentially malicious activity such as compromised instances or unusual API calls. Which service should they enable?

choices.text: AWS Config
AWS Trusted Advisor
Amazon Macie
Amazon GuardDuty

explanation:
Why this is correct:
GuardDuty continuously analyzes VPC flow logs, DNS logs, and CloudTrail events for threats.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config: configuration compliance.
• Trusted Advisor: best practices.
• Macie: sensitive data in S3.

Key takeaway: threat detection → GuardDuty.

stem: A company must find which of its 400 S3 buckets contain passport numbers and credit card data, and get alerts when new sensitive data appears. Which service fits BEST?

choices.text: AWS Config rules checking bucket encryption
Amazon Macie automated discovery
Amazon GuardDuty S3 Protection findings
Amazon Inspector scans of the buckets' contents

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Macie discovers and classifies sensitive data in S3 using managed data identifiers (such as passport and card numbers) and publishes findings for new discoveries.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Inspector: finds software vulnerabilities, not data content.
• Config encryption rules: encryption status says nothing about whether data is sensitive.
• GuardDuty S3 Protection: detects suspicious access activity, not data content.

Key takeaway: what's IN the S3 data → Macie; who is ACCESSING it suspiciously → GuardDuty.

stem: A mobile application needs to let end users sign up, sign in, and manage their own profiles, and the development team wants a fully managed service to handle this user directory and authentication flow, including social identity provider login. Which service should they use?

choices.text: AWS IAM Identity Center
AWS Directory Service
AWS Organizations
Amazon Cognito user pools

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cognito user pools provide sign-up, sign-in, and profile management for application users.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Identity Center: workforce access to AWS.
• Directory Service: Microsoft AD.
• Organizations: accounts.

Key takeaway: customer app users → Cognito.

stem: An application on an EC2 instance cannot receive inbound HTTPS traffic from clients on the internet, even though the instance has a public IP address and the route table has a route to an internet gateway. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: NAT gateways block inbound HTTPS traffic to instances in any subnet
The instance's security group lacks an inbound rule for TCP 443
The VPC does not support HTTPS traffic without additional configuration
The instance is in a different Region from the clients' DNS records

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A security group without an inbound rule for TCP 443 blocks HTTPS even when the instance has a public IP.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NAT gateways: don't block inbound traffic to public instances.
• VPC doesn't support HTTPS: it does.
• Region mismatch: irrelevant.

Key takeaway: inbound access requires an SG rule.

stem: A financial services company needs a dedicated, private network connection between its data center and AWS with consistent low latency and high bandwidth for a latency-sensitive trading application, and is willing to accept a longer setup lead time to achieve this. Which connectivity option best fits this requirement compared to a Site-to-Site VPN?

choices.text: Amazon CloudFront, because it caches content closer to users
AWS Transit Gateway alone, without any on-premises connectivity
AWS Direct Connect, a dedicated private link with consistent performance
AWS Site-to-Site VPN, because it can be provisioned in minutes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Direct Connect provides a dedicated private link with consistent latency and bandwidth.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudFront: content delivery.
• Transit Gateway alone: no on-premises link.
• VPN: internet-based and variable.

Key takeaway: consistent private hybrid link → Direct Connect.

stem: Instances in a private subnet can't reach the internet. The subnet's route table has only the local route. A NAT gateway exists in a public subnet. What fixes this?

choices.text: Add 0.0.0.0/0 pointing to the internet gateway in the private subnet's route table
Add a route to the NAT gateway in the public subnet's route table
Add 0.0.0.0/0 pointing to the NAT gateway in the private subnet's route table
Attach a security group to the NAT gateway allowing outbound traffic

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Route tables decide where traffic from a subnet goes. The private subnet needs a default route to the NAT gateway, which forwards through the internet gateway from its public subnet.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Route to IGW from the private subnet: makes the subnet public, which needs public IPs and exposes instances.
• SG on the NAT gateway: NAT gateways don't use security groups.
• Route in the public subnet: the public subnet already routes to the IGW; the private subnet is the problem.

Key takeaway: subnets are public or private because of their route tables.

stem: A network engineer adds a NACL rule with rule number 100 to deny all inbound traffic from a specific IP range, but traffic from that range is still reaching instances in the subnet. The NACL already has a rule with number 50 that allows all inbound traffic. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: Security groups always override NACL rules, so the deny is ignored
NACL rules are evaluated in reverse order of their rule numbers
NACLs do not support deny rules, so rule 100 has no effect
Rules are evaluated lowest number first, so rule 50 matches first

explanation:
Why this is correct:
NACL rules are evaluated from the lowest number and the first match wins, so an existing rule 50 that allows the range is applied before the deny at rule 100.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SGs override NACLs: both apply.
• Reverse order: incorrect.
• No deny rules: NACLs support deny.

Key takeaway: put NACL denies at lower numbers.

stem: A company runs a public-facing web application and wants to build a layered defense against both large-scale volumetric DDoS attacks and application-layer attacks like HTTP floods and malicious request patterns. Which combination of services provides this defense in depth?

choices.text: CloudFront and Shield Advanced at the edge, plus AWS WAF
Security groups alone, restricting inbound ports to 80 and 443
Amazon Macie and AWS Config for continuous threat monitoring
AWS Direct Connect and AWS Trusted Advisor for traffic isolation

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront and Shield Advanced absorb volumetric attacks at the edge, and WAF filters application-layer attacks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Security groups alone: no DDoS absorption.
• Macie and Config: not defenses.
• Direct Connect and Trusted Advisor: not DDoS controls.

Key takeaway: layered DDoS defense at the edge.

stem: A company is deciding between using a NAT gateway and a self-managed NAT instance to provide outbound internet access for private subnet resources. Which statement accurately compares the two?

choices.text: A NAT instance is managed by AWS, while a NAT gateway must be patched manually
NAT instances and NAT gateways have identical management overhead
A NAT gateway is managed and highly available; a NAT instance needs patching and scaling
NAT gateways cannot scale bandwidth, unlike NAT instances

explanation:
Why this is correct:
NAT gateways are managed, highly available in an AZ, and scale automatically. NAT instances need patching, scaling, and failover handling.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NAT instance managed by AWS: reversed.
• Identical overhead: they differ.
• Gateways can't scale: they scale.

Key takeaway: prefer managed NAT gateways.

stem: A three-tier app places web servers in public subnets and app servers and databases in private subnets. An auditor asks what actually prevents internet users from reaching the database directly. What is the BEST answer?

choices.text: The database has no public DNS name, so it can't be discovered from the internet
The VPC's CIDR range is private, so internet traffic can't be addressed to it
The NAT gateway blocks all inbound connections to private subnets
The DB subnet has no IGW route, and its SG allows only the app tier's SG

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Defense in depth: without an internet gateway route and public IP, there's no inbound path from the internet, and the security group limits access to the app tier.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No public DNS name: obscurity isn't a control.
• NAT gateway: enables outbound only; it isn't the reason inbound fails, and it doesn't filter.
• Private CIDR alone: instances with public IPs in routed subnets are reachable despite private VPC ranges.

Key takeaway: isolation comes from routing plus security groups, not from names or address ranges.

stem: A security team wants to block common SQL injection and cross-site scripting (XSS) patterns in incoming web requests without writing custom detection logic from scratch. What is the most efficient way to achieve this with AWS WAF?

choices.text: A custom Lambda function for every possible attack signature
A NACL configured to inspect HTTP payloads for attack patterns
AWS Managed Rules for WAF (SQL database, Core Rule Set)
Disable WAF and rely on security groups to block malicious requests

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS Managed Rules for WAF (such as the SQL database and Core rule sets) block common SQL injection and XSS patterns without writing rules.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Custom Lambda per signature: heavy and unnecessary.
• NACL payload inspection: NACLs don't inspect payloads.
• Disabling WAF: removes protection.

Key takeaway: common web attacks → WAF managed rules.

stem: An application architecture has a web tier and a database tier, both running on Auto Scaling groups whose instances change frequently. Which security group configuration best accommodates this dynamic scaling while maintaining least privilege?

choices.text: Allow inbound traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 on the database port
Reference the web tier's security group as the source
Remove the database security group and rely on NACLs instead
Update the database IP allow list manually whenever instances change

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Referencing the web tier's security group as the source allows any current or future web instance without IP maintenance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• 0.0.0.0/0: exposes the database.
• NACLs only: can't reference groups.
• Manual IP lists: break with scaling.

Key takeaway: reference security groups for dynamic tiers.

stem: A company needs to establish secure connectivity between its on-premises network and a VPC within a few hours, with encryption in transit, and can tolerate variable latency since the workload is not latency-sensitive. Which option best meets this need?

choices.text: Amazon CloudFront in front of the on-premises network
AWS Site-to-Site VPN (IPsec over the internet)
A VPC peering connection to another company VPC
AWS Direct Connect, which can be provisioned within hours

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Site-to-Site VPN is set up in hours and encrypts traffic with IPsec over the internet.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudFront: not connectivity.
• VPC peering: VPC to VPC.
• Direct Connect: takes weeks and isn't encrypted by default.

Key takeaway: fast encrypted hybrid link → VPN.

stem: A bucket uses SSE-KMS with a customer managed key. Uploads of many small objects start failing with ThrottlingException from KMS during peak hours. What reduces KMS calls without weakening encryption?

choices.text: Switch to SSE-C with client-supplied keys
Enable S3 Bucket Keys for SSE-KMS
Request encryption only on download to halve requests
Use a separate KMS key per object to spread the load

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SSE-KMS uses envelope encryption, generating a data key through KMS for objects. Bucket Keys create a short-lived bucket-level key from KMS and derive object data keys from it, cutting KMS requests (and cost) substantially while keeping KMS-backed encryption.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SSE-C: moves key management to the client, a big change that isn't needed.
• Encrypt on download: S3 encrypts at write; this option doesn't exist.
• Key per object: more keys to manage, and it doesn't reduce request volume.

Key takeaway: high-volume SSE-KMS → Bucket Keys.

stem: A company needs free public TLS certificates for an ALB and a CloudFront distribution that renew automatically. Which approach fits, and what is required for CloudFront?

choices.text: ACM certificates exported and installed on the ALB targets; CloudFront uses the same Region's certificate
KMS asymmetric keys configured as TLS keys on both the ALB and CloudFront
Certificates stored in Secrets Manager with a rotation Lambda that re-imports them
ACM certificates with DNS validation; the CloudFront certificate must be in us-east-1

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ACM issues free public certificates for integrated services and renews them automatically when DNS validation stays in place. CloudFront uses certificates from us-east-1.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Exporting public ACM certificates: public ACM certificates can't be exported, and CloudFront needs us-east-1.
• KMS keys: KMS doesn't provide TLS certificates to load balancers.
• Secrets Manager rotation: unnecessary work when ACM renews automatically.

Key takeaway: ALB/CloudFront TLS → ACM (CloudFront certs in us-east-1).

stem: A company uses AWS Certificate Manager to issue a public certificate for its Application Load Balancer and wants to avoid manual certificate renewal and the risk of an expired certificate causing an outage. What should they do?

choices.text: Use an ACM-issued certificate, which ACM renews automatically
Track the expiration date manually and re-issue the certificate each year
Switch to a self-signed certificate to avoid renewal entirely
Export the certificate and install it on each server behind the ALB

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ACM-issued public certificates used with integrated services such as ALB renew automatically (with DNS validation in place).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual tracking: the error to avoid.
• Self-signed: browsers don't trust it.
• Exporting to servers: public ACM certificates can't be exported.

Key takeaway: ALB TLS without renewals → ACM.

stem: A user has an IAM policy that grants kms:Decrypt on a specific KMS key, but the user still receives an Access Denied error when attempting to decrypt data with that key. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: The key policy doesn't allow the principal; both key policy and IAM must allow it
IAM policies never apply to KMS keys, only key policies do
The key is in a different Region from the caller's credentials
KMS keys cannot be used for decryption through the API

explanation:
Why this is correct:
KMS requires the key policy to allow access (directly or by enabling IAM policies). If the key policy doesn't, the IAM allow alone doesn't work.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM never applies: it does when the key policy enables it.
• Region mismatch: possible, but not the stated issue.
• KMS can't decrypt via API: it can.

Key takeaway: KMS access = key policy + IAM.

stem: A company wants to protect critical S3 data against accidental deletion and also maintain a copy in a second AWS Region for disaster recovery. Which combination of features should be enabled?

choices.text: S3 Intelligent-Tiering with archive access tiers
S3 Versioning plus Cross-Region Replication
S3 Transfer Acceleration to a second bucket
Removing bucket policies to allow restores

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Versioning keeps prior versions if objects are deleted or overwritten, and Cross-Region Replication maintains a copy in another Region.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Intelligent-Tiering: cost, not protection.
• Transfer Acceleration: speed.
• Removing bucket policies: weakens security.

Key takeaway: accidental deletion + DR → Versioning + CRR.

stem: A company wants encryption, access, and retention controls applied automatically according to how sensitive each dataset is. What must it do FIRST, and how can AWS help?

choices.text: Move all data to the cheapest storage class, then classify what remains
Encrypt everything with one KMS key, then decide on classification later
Classify and tag data by sensitivity; Macie helps find it
Apply the strictest controls to all data

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Classification decides which controls apply. Tags (for example, classification=confidential) let policies and automation act on it, and Macie helps discover sensitive data that isn't labeled yet.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One key first: skips the step that tells you which data needs stronger controls.
• Cheapest storage first: cost optimization before knowing sensitivity risks non-compliance.
• Strictest for everything: costly and often impractical; controls should match sensitivity.

Key takeaway: classify first; controls follow the classification.

stem: A company runs workloads using EBS volumes, RDS databases, and DynamoDB tables and wants to centrally define and enforce backup schedules, retention periods, and cross-region copy policies across all of these resource types from a single service. Which service should they use?

choices.text: AWS Config
Amazon S3 Glacier
AWS Backup
AWS Trusted Advisor

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS Backup centrally defines backup plans and retention for EBS, RDS, DynamoDB, and more.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config: compliance.
• Glacier: storage class.
• Trusted Advisor: recommendations.

Key takeaway: central backup policies → AWS Backup.

stem: Account A wants to allow a role in Account B to decrypt objects encrypted with a customer managed KMS key owned by Account A. The role in Account B has an IAM policy allowing kms:Decrypt, but decryption still fails. What additional configuration is most likely missing?

choices.text: The S3 bucket policy must allow kms:Decrypt for the Account B role
KMS keys can never be shared across accounts
Account B needs a Direct Connect connection to Account A
The key policy must allow the external account or role

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The key policy in Account A must allow the external account or role (and Account B's IAM must also allow kms:Decrypt).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bucket policy grants KMS: KMS permissions come from key policies.
• Keys can't be shared: they can.
• Direct Connect: irrelevant.

Key takeaway: cross-account KMS → key policy.

stem: A financial company must retain certain records in Amazon S3 in a way that prevents them from being deleted or overwritten by any user, including the root account, for a fixed retention period, to meet regulatory requirements. Which S3 feature should be used?

choices.text: S3 Object Lock in compliance mode
S3 Transfer Acceleration
S3 bucket policies alone
S3 Standard-Infrequent Access storage class

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Object Lock in compliance mode prevents deletion or overwriting by any user, including root, until retention expires.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Transfer Acceleration: speed.
• Bucket policies: can be changed by admins.
• Standard-IA: storage class.

Key takeaway: immutable records → Object Lock compliance mode.

stem: A company wants to encrypt all new EBS volumes in an account by default using a customer managed KMS key rather than the AWS managed default key, without requiring developers to manually specify encryption settings each time. What should they configure?

choices.text: Disable KMS and rely on S3 default encryption for all stored data
Attach an IAM policy that requires encryption on CreateVolume calls
Manually re-encrypt each volume with the key after creation
Enable EBS encryption by default with the customer managed key

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EBS encryption by default, with a customer managed key set as the default, encrypts all new volumes automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 default encryption: doesn't cover EBS.
• IAM condition: blocks but doesn't encrypt.
• Manual re-encryption: error-prone.

Key takeaway: automatic EBS encryption → encryption by default.

stem: A company needs full control over a KMS key's access policy, the ability to enable or disable the key, and the ability to define custom key rotation and deletion schedules, in order to meet a strict compliance requirement. Which type of KMS key should they use?

choices.text: A customer managed key
There is no difference between the three key types for this purpose
An AWS owned key
An AWS managed key

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Customer managed keys give full control of key policy, enable/disable, and rotation settings.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No difference: key types differ.
• AWS owned keys: no customer control.
• AWS managed keys: limited control.

Key takeaway: key control → customer managed keys.

stem: An auditor asks a company for AWS's SOC 2 report and the AWS PCI DSS attestation, and also asks whether the company's own accounts meet PCI controls. Which services answer each request?

choices.text: AWS Config for AWS's reports; Amazon Inspector for the accounts
Artifact for AWS's reports; Security Hub for the accounts
Security Hub for AWS's reports; AWS Artifact for checking the accounts
Trusted Advisor for both requests

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Artifact provides AWS's own compliance reports and agreements. Security Hub's PCI DSS standard checks the customer's accounts against controls.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Swapped roles: Security Hub checks your environment; Artifact holds AWS's reports.
• Trusted Advisor: best-practice checks, not compliance reports or PCI mapping.
• Config and Inspector: neither provides AWS audit reports; Inspector finds vulnerabilities.

Key takeaway: AWS's compliance evidence → Artifact; your compliance posture → Security Hub/Config.

stem: A company generates large volumes of log data in S3 that are frequently accessed for 30 days, rarely accessed for the next 60 days, and then must be retained for 7 years for compliance at the lowest possible cost, with retrieval times of several hours being acceptable. Which S3 feature should be used to automate this data lifecycle?

choices.text: S3 Transfer Acceleration
S3 Cross-Region Replication
Lifecycle to Standard-IA, then Glacier Deep Archive
S3 Requester Pays

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A lifecycle policy moves logs to Standard-IA after 30 days and to Glacier Deep Archive after 90 days, matching the access pattern at the lowest cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Transfer Acceleration: speed.
• CRR: replication.
• Requester Pays: billing.

Key takeaway: access declines over time → lifecycle transitions.

stem: A company configured S3 Cross-Region Replication for a bucket encrypted with a customer managed KMS key, but replicated objects in the destination Region fail to decrypt properly for applications there. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The destination bucket must be unencrypted for replication to succeed
Cross-Region Replication does not support encrypted objects at all
The replication rule needs a destination-Region key (or a multi-Region key)
IAM roles cannot be used with S3 replication, so a bucket policy is required

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Replicating SSE-KMS objects requires the replication rule to specify a KMS key in the destination Region (or a multi-Region key), and the replication role needs permission to use both keys.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Destination must be unencrypted: not required.
• CRR doesn't support encryption: it does.
• IAM roles can't be used: replication uses an IAM role.

Key takeaway: KMS + CRR → destination key and role permissions.

stem: A company in a highly regulated industry must use a dedicated, single-tenant hardware security module where they retain sole administrative control over the HSM, rather than a shared multi-tenant key management service. Which AWS service meets this requirement?

choices.text: AWS CloudHSM
AWS Certificate Manager
Amazon Macie
AWS KMS with AWS managed keys

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudHSM provides dedicated, single-tenant HSMs where the customer has sole administrative control of keys.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ACM: certificates.
• Macie: data discovery.
• KMS with AWS managed keys: shared, AWS-controlled.

Key takeaway: single-tenant HSM → CloudHSM.

stem: Data flows from browsers to an ALB, from the ALB to EC2, and into RDS. Policy requires encryption everywhere. Which set of controls covers both at rest and in transit?

choices.text: A VPN from browsers to the VPC, with no storage encryption needed
HTTPS on the ALB listener only, plus KMS encryption on RDS
KMS encryption on EBS and RDS, since stored data is where breaches occur
TLS on every hop, plus KMS encryption for EBS and RDS

explanation:
Why this is correct:
In transit covers every hop: client to ALB, ALB to targets (HTTPS to targets), and app to database (TLS). At rest covers stored data: EBS volumes and RDS storage with KMS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ALB listener only: the ALB-to-target and app-to-database hops stay unencrypted.
• Storage only: leaves network hops exposed.
• VPN from browsers: impractical for public users and ignores data at rest.

Key takeaway: list each hop and each store; each needs its own encryption.

stem: A company's disaster recovery plan requires a Recovery Point Objective (RPO) of near-zero data loss and a Recovery Time Objective (RTO) of a few minutes for a critical relational database, in the event an entire AWS Region becomes unavailable. Which approach best supports these objectives?

choices.text: A cross-Region replica (or Aurora Global Database) promoted in the DR Region
Multi-AZ within a single Region, which also protects against Regional failure
Nightly manual database snapshots copied to another Region
Weekly exports to S3 Glacier Deep Archive in a second Region

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Near-zero RPO with fast Regional recovery needs continuous cross-Region replication, such as a cross-Region replica or Aurora Global Database, promoted during a disaster.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Multi-AZ: protects against AZ failures, not Regional ones.
• Nightly snapshots: up to a day of data loss.
• Weekly exports: far too much loss.

Key takeaway: Regional DR with near-zero RPO → cross-Region replication.

stem: A serverless application receives bursty traffic that occasionally exceeds the backend Lambda function's concurrency, causing downstream throttling. The architect wants API Gateway to smooth incoming traffic spikes before they reach Lambda, without changing client behavior. Which configuration should be used?

choices.text: Move the API behind an S3 static website endpoint
A usage plan with rate and burst throttling
Enable API Gateway response caching for all methods
Set the Lambda function's reserved concurrency to unlimited

explanation:
Why this is correct:
API Gateway usage plans with rate and burst throttling limit incoming traffic so the backend isn't overwhelmed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 website: not an API.
• Caching all methods: not all responses are cacheable.
• Unlimited concurrency: not an option and can overload downstream.

Key takeaway: protect backends with throttling.

stem: A financial partner requires SFTP access to exchange files, but the company wants uploaded files to land directly in Amazon S3 without operating any SFTP servers themselves. Which service meets this requirement?

choices.text: AWS Transfer Family
AWS Storage Gateway
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
AWS DataSync

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Transfer Family provides SFTP endpoints that store files directly in S3.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Storage Gateway: on-premises access to AWS storage.
• FSx for Windows: SMB.
• DataSync: transfers, not partner SFTP.

Key takeaway: SFTP into S3 → Transfer Family.

stem: A product catalog in RDS MySQL is read thousands of times per second and changes a few times per hour. Stale data up to 5 minutes is acceptable. Which design cuts read load MOST?

choices.text: CloudFront in front of the RDS endpoint
A larger RDS instance class with more memory
ElastiCache cache-aside with a 5-minute TTL
Global Accelerator in front of the application

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A cache-aside layer in ElastiCache serves repeated reads from memory, and a TTL bounds staleness to the acceptable 5 minutes, sharply reducing database queries.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudFront: caches HTTP responses at edges; it can't sit in front of a database connection.
• Bigger instance: more capacity, but every read still hits the database.
• Global Accelerator: improves network paths, not database load.

Key takeaway: hot, rarely changing reads with tolerable staleness → cache with a TTL.

stem: An architect is choosing between a write-through and a lazy-loading (cache-aside) strategy for an ElastiCache layer in front of a database. Which statement correctly describes a tradeoff of the write-through strategy?

choices.text: Write-through keeps the cache current but adds write latency and unread data
Lazy loading writes every database update into the cache before the write completes
Write-through removes the need to set a TTL on any cached items
Lazy loading guarantees that the cache never contains stale data

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Write-through keeps the cache current but adds write latency and can fill the cache with data that's never read. Lazy loading caches only what's requested but can serve stale data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lazy loading writes updates first: that's write-through.
• No TTL needed: TTLs still help.
• Lazy loading never stale: it can be.

Key takeaway: write-through = fresh but heavier; lazy = efficient but possibly stale.

stem: Which statement best differentiates Amazon SNS from Amazon SQS in an event-driven architecture?

choices.text: SNS pushes to many subscribers; SQS holds messages until consumers poll
SNS and SQS provide identical delivery models and are fully interchangeable
SQS pushes messages to subscribers, while SNS requires consumers to poll
SNS guarantees exactly-once processing

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SNS pushes messages to many subscribers at once. SQS stores messages until consumers poll and process them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Interchangeable: different models.
• Reversed: SQS is pull-based.
• Exactly-once: SNS doesn't guarantee it.

Key takeaway: push fan-out → SNS; buffered pull → SQS.

stem: An app on one EC2 instance hits CPU limits. The team resizes it to a larger type, which requires a stop and start. They now want to handle future growth without downtime. What is the recommended next step?

choices.text: Move the instance to a placement group so it can use more CPU
Scale horizontally: an Auto Scaling group across AZs behind a load balancer
Enable detailed monitoring so the instance can grow its vCPU count automatically
Keep scaling vertically, scheduling a larger instance type each month

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The resize was vertical scaling, which has a ceiling and needs a restart. Horizontal scaling adds instances with no downtime and removes the single point of failure.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Monthly vertical resizes: keep the downtime and the ceiling.
• Detailed monitoring: more frequent metrics; it doesn't change capacity.
• Placement groups: affect network placement, not CPU.

Key takeaway: vertical = bigger box with limits and restarts; horizontal = more boxes.

stem: A stateless web tier must handle unpredictable traffic spikes with minimal risk of downtime if any single component fails. Compared to repeatedly resizing one instance, which scaling strategy is generally preferred for this goal?

choices.text: Horizontal scaling with an Auto Scaling group across AZs
Consolidating onto a single larger on-premises server
Disabling health checks so instances are never replaced
Vertical scaling by upgrading to larger instance types

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Horizontal scaling across AZs handles spikes and survives the loss of any single instance or AZ.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Single server: single point of failure.
• No health checks: failed instances remain.
• Vertical scaling: limits and downtime.

Key takeaway: resilience and elasticity → scale out across AZs.

stem: A video platform serves the same 2-10 GB files worldwide from S3 in one Region. Latency is high far from the Region, and egress costs are rising. Which service addresses both issues?

choices.text: CloudFront with the S3 bucket as origin
S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket
AWS Global Accelerator in front of the bucket
Cross-Region Replication to every Region

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront caches content at edge locations close to viewers, reducing latency and origin requests. Transfer from S3 to CloudFront is free, and CloudFront delivery is typically cheaper than direct S3 egress.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Transfer Acceleration: speeds uploads (and some downloads) via edges but doesn't cache.
• Replication everywhere: multiplies storage cost and still has no caching.
• Global Accelerator: optimizes TCP/UDP paths to endpoints; it isn't a CDN cache.

Key takeaway: repeatable content for global viewers → CloudFront.

stem: One domain must route /api/* to a container service, /images/* to a Lambda function, and requests with header X-Version: beta to a canary group. Which load balancer supports all of this natively?

choices.text: Network Load Balancer with separate listeners on different ports
Gateway Load Balancer with target groups per path
Classic Load Balancer with sticky sessions
Application Load Balancer with listener rules

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ALB listener rules match on path, host, and HTTP headers, and ALB supports Lambda functions as targets.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NLB: Layer 4, so it can't inspect paths or headers.
• GWLB: for inline network appliances, not HTTP routing.
• CLB: legacy, with no content-based routing.

Key takeaway: HTTP content-based routing (path, host, header) → ALB.

stem: A company is designing a three-tier web app that must scale each tier independently, keep the database private, and serve static assets globally. Which mapping fits BEST?

choices.text: CloudFront + S3 and an ALB; app ASG; private Aurora
One large EC2 instance running web, app, and database, behind CloudFront
S3 for the web tier, Route 53 for app logic, and DynamoDB exposed publicly
An ALB in private subnets

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Each tier scales on its own: the edge serves static files, the ALB spreads traffic, Auto Scaling scales the app tier, and a managed database stays in private subnets.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One instance: no independent scaling and a single point of failure.
• Route 53 as app logic: DNS isn't compute, and a public database is exposed.
• Inverted placement: public app servers and databases expose them.

Key takeaway: separate tiers so each scales and is secured independently.

stem: A team needs to run a long-running batch container process, lasting several hours and requiring more memory than AWS Lambda's maximum, without managing any servers. Which service is more appropriate than Lambda?

choices.text: AWS Fargate
An EC2 Spot Fleet managed entirely by custom scaling scripts
Amazon S3 Batch Operations
AWS Lambda with its timeout extended beyond 15 minutes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Fargate runs containers for hours with more memory than Lambda allows, without managing servers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Custom Spot scripts: more work.
• S3 Batch Operations: object operations.
• Lambda beyond 15 minutes: not possible.

Key takeaway: long, memory-heavy containers → Fargate.

stem: A Lambda function that processes S3 upload events intermittently times out under heavy concurrent load, and CloudWatch metrics show a high number of throttled invocations. What is the most likely cause and remedy?

choices.text: The bucket lacks durability; enabling versioning will fix the throttling
Concurrency limits are reached; raise the quota or set reserved concurrency
The event source is throttled by an expired IAM access key
The function needs a larger attached EBS volume for the images

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Throttles show the function hit its concurrency limit. Raise the account quota or set reserved concurrency for the function.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Versioning: unrelated.
• Expired access key: S3 events use service permissions.
• EBS volume: Lambda doesn't use EBS.

Key takeaway: throttled Lambda → concurrency limits.

stem: Hundreds of Linux instances in three AZs must share a POSIX file system for content that is read often but rarely changed, at the lowest cost. Which option fits BEST?

choices.text: Amazon S3 mounted as a file system on every instance
Amazon EBS Multi-Attach io2 volumes shared by all instances
FSx for Windows File Server with SMB shares
Amazon EFS with lifecycle to Infrequent Access

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EFS is a regional, multi-AZ POSIX file system mountable by many Linux clients. Lifecycle management moves colder files to the lower-cost Infrequent Access class.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EBS Multi-Attach: limited to a few instances in one AZ and needs a cluster-aware file system.
• S3 as a file system: not POSIX-compliant; mount tools have semantic limitations.
• FSx for Windows: SMB for Windows workloads, not the natural fit for Linux POSIX sharing.

Key takeaway: shared POSIX files across AZs → EFS; cost → lifecycle to IA.

stem: A self-managed database on EC2 needs 60,000 IOPS with consistent sub-millisecond latency on one volume and 99.999% durability. Which storage fits BEST?

choices.text: EBS io2 Block Express
EC2 instance store NVMe volumes
EBS gp3 at 60,000 IOPS
Amazon EFS in Max I/O mode

explanation:
Why this is correct:
io2 Block Express supports very high IOPS per volume with consistent sub-millisecond latency and 99.999% durability, which suits critical databases.

Why the other options are wrong:
• gp3: supports up to 16,000 IOPS per volume.
• EFS: a network file system with higher latency, not block storage for a single database.
• Instance store: fast but ephemeral; data is lost if the instance stops or fails.

Key takeaway: highest, most consistent block performance plus durability → io2 Block Express.

stem: An ECS workload must always run 4 copies of a task behind an ALB, replace failed tasks, and roll out new versions gradually. Which ECS construct provides this?

choices.text: A task definition with 4 container definitions
An ECS service with desired count 4 and a load balancer
The ECS container agent's restart policy on each instance
A standalone RunTask call scheduled every minute

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An ECS service maintains the desired number of running tasks, replaces failed ones, registers them with the load balancer, and manages rolling or blue/green deployments.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scheduled RunTask: launches tasks but doesn't maintain a count or integrate with deployments.
• Four containers in one task definition: that's one task with four containers, not four copies.
• Agent restart policy: restarts containers on one instance, not service-level replacement or deployments.

Key takeaway: long-running, self-healing, load-balanced tasks → ECS service.

stem: A read-heavy reporting workload is degrading performance on the primary RDS MySQL instance that also handles transactional writes. What is the most effective way to offload the read traffic without impacting write performance?

choices.text: Enable a Multi-AZ standby and send reporting queries to it
Increase the primary instance's allocated storage size
Add read replicas for the reporting queries
Move the workload to a single, larger instance class

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Read replicas take reporting queries off the primary, which keeps handling writes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Multi-AZ standby: not readable in the instance deployment.
• More storage: doesn't reduce query load.
• One bigger instance: still shared.

Key takeaway: offload reads → read replicas.

stem: A photo-sharing application processes uploaded images through resizing, watermarking, and thumbnail-generation steps. The architect wants each step to scale independently and remain resilient to failures in the other steps. Which approach best achieves this loose coupling?

choices.text: A single monolithic Lambda function invoked synchronously by the upload handler
Run all processing steps on one EC2 instance to simplify communication
Direct in-process function calls between the three processing components
Separate SQS queues or events between independent workers

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Queues or events between independent workers let each step scale and fail independently, with retries.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Monolithic Lambda: coupled and limited.
• One EC2 instance: single point of failure.
• In-process calls: tight coupling.

Key takeaway: decouple pipeline steps.

stem: A company wants a database to survive the loss of a single data center facility with automatic failover, but keep synchronous replication latency low. Across which boundary should it replicate?

choices.text: Across AWS Regions
Across Availability Zones
Across racks in one Availability Zone
Across edge locations

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AZs are physically separate facilities with independent power and networking, connected by low-latency links, which is the right boundary for synchronous high availability.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Across Regions: much higher latency; used for DR with async replication.
• Edge locations: don't host databases.
• Racks in one AZ: an AZ-level event takes them all down.

Key takeaway: synchronous HA boundary = Availability Zone.

stem: A company wants DNS-based failover so that if the primary application endpoint in one Region becomes unhealthy, traffic automatically routes to a standby endpoint in another Region. Which Route 53 routing policy should be used?

choices.text: Geolocation routing policy
Simple routing policy
Failover routing policy
Multivalue answer routing policy

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Failover routing sends traffic to the secondary endpoint when the primary's health check fails.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Geolocation: routes by location.
• Simple: no health-based failover.
• Multivalue: returns multiple records, not active-passive failover.

Key takeaway: active-passive DNS → failover routing.

stem: An accessibility feature must read support articles aloud in several languages, with some words pronounced in a custom way, and generate audio files cached for reuse. Which service fits BEST?

choices.text: Amazon Transcribe with custom vocabularies
Amazon Comprehend with custom entities
Amazon Polly with custom lexicons
Amazon Translate with custom terminology

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Polly converts text to speech in many languages. Lexicons control pronunciation, and synthesized audio can be stored in S3 and reused.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Transcribe: speech to text, the opposite direction.
• Translate: text to text between languages; no audio.
• Comprehend: text analytics, no speech output.

Key takeaway: text → speech = Polly; speech → text = Transcribe.

stem: EC2 instances in a private subnet cannot reach the internet through a NAT gateway, even though the NAT gateway is running and has an Elastic IP address. What is the most likely misconfiguration to check first?

choices.text: A security group attached to the NAT gateway is blocking outbound traffic
The private instances are missing their own Elastic IP addresses
The internet gateway is attached to the private subnet instead of the public one
The private route table lacks a 0.0.0.0/0 route to the NAT gateway

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Private subnets need a 0.0.0.0/0 route to the NAT gateway in their route table.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NAT gateway security group: NAT gateways don't use SGs.
• Private instance EIPs: not needed.
• IGW on the private subnet: gateways attach to VPCs, not subnets.

Key takeaway: private internet access = route to NAT.

stem: A VPC has a public subnet that must reach the internet directly and a private subnet that must reach the internet only through a NAT gateway. Which statement correctly describes the required route table configuration?

choices.text: Public: 0.0.0.0/0 to IGW; private: 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT gateway in the public subnet
Both subnets should have a 0.0.0.0/0 route pointing directly to the internet gateway
The private subnet routes to the internet gateway; the public subnet routes via the NAT gateway
Only the main route table needs configuration; subnet route tables are unnecessary

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The public subnet routes 0.0.0.0/0 to the internet gateway, and the private subnet routes 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT gateway in the public subnet.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Both to IGW: the private subnet becomes public.
• Reversed: incorrect.
• Main table only: subnets need correct associations.

Key takeaway: routing defines public vs. private.

stem: An app needs RPO in minutes and RTO under an hour at low cost. The plan: keep a replica database running in a second Region and provision app servers from AMIs only during a disaster. Which DR strategy is this?

choices.text: Multi-site active-active
Warm standby
Pilot light
Backup and restore

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Pilot light keeps only the core data layer running and replicated; the rest is provisioned quickly during failover. This gives minutes of RPO and a sub-hour RTO at low standing cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Warm standby: a scaled-down but fully running stack.
• Backup and restore: nothing runs; data is restored from backups, so recovery is slower.
• Active-active: full capacity in both Regions.

Key takeaway: only data running = pilot light; everything running small = warm standby.

stem: A company wants the lowest possible RTO and RPO and is willing to pay to run full production capacity simultaneously in two Regions, actively serving live traffic from both. Which DR strategy does this describe?

choices.text: Multi-site active-active
Pilot light
Backup and restore
Warm standby

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Running full capacity in two Regions simultaneously (multi-site active-active) gives the lowest RTO and RPO.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Pilot light, backup and restore, warm standby: longer recovery.

Key takeaway: lowest RTO/RPO → active-active.

stem: A company's disaster recovery plan states that after an incident, it can tolerate losing up to 1 hour of data and must restore service within 4 hours. Which pair of terms correctly describes these two targets, respectively?

choices.text: RTO of 1 hour, RPO of 4 hours
SLA of 1 hour, SLO of 4 hours
RPO of 1 hour, RTO of 4 hours
MTTR of 1 hour, MTBF of 4 hours

explanation:
Why this is correct:
RPO is the acceptable data loss (1 hour). RTO is the acceptable time to restore service (4 hours).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Swapped: incorrect.
• SLA/SLO: service commitments, not DR objectives.
• MTTR/MTBF: reliability metrics.

Key takeaway: RPO = data; RTO = time.

stem: A company is choosing between a warm standby and a pilot light disaster recovery strategy for a critical application. Which statement correctly describes a key tradeoff between the two?

choices.text: Warm standby runs a scaled-down working copy, recovering faster at higher cost
Warm standby keeps no compute running until failover, so it costs less than pilot light
Pilot light and warm standby have identical RTO and cost profiles
Pilot light keeps full production capacity running at all times in the DR Region

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Warm standby runs a scaled-down but working copy, so it recovers faster than pilot light at higher cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No compute in warm standby: incorrect.
• Identical: they differ.
• Pilot light full capacity: incorrect.

Key takeaway: warm standby = running small; pilot light = core data only.

stem: A payment service calls a partner API that sometimes returns 503. Retries currently happen immediately in a loop, worsening the outage. The team also wants to stop calling after sustained failures. Which combination fits?

choices.text: Fan-out to three copies of the request
Backoff with jitter plus a circuit breaker
Immediate retries with a higher attempt limit
A bulkhead that doubles the thread pool

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Backoff with jitter spreads retries so a recovering service isn't overwhelmed. A circuit breaker stops calls after repeated failures and probes later, protecting both sides during extended outages.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More immediate retries: amplifies load during an outage.
• Fan-out: triples load on the failing dependency.
• Bigger bulkhead: isolates resources but doesn't reduce retry pressure.

Key takeaway: transient → backoff with jitter; sustained → circuit breaker.

stem: An RDS Multi-AZ DB instance's primary fails. The application uses the RDS endpoint name but caches DNS results for 1 hour. What happens, and what should be fixed?

choices.text: RDS promotes a read replica with a new endpoint that must be configured
The standby serves reads during failover, so no change is needed
RDS fails over and updates the endpoint's DNS; fix the app's DNS caching
The application must restore from a snapshot, since Multi-AZ doesn't fail over automatically

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Multi-AZ fails over to the synchronous standby automatically and repoints the same DNS name. Clients that cache DNS longer than the record's short TTL keep connecting to the old IP.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Read replica promotion: that's a manual pattern with a new endpoint, not Multi-AZ.
• Snapshot restore: Multi-AZ fails over automatically.
• Standby serving reads: a Multi-AZ DB instance standby isn't readable.

Key takeaway: Multi-AZ changes the IP behind the same name, so clients must respect DNS TTL.

stem: An application uses Route 53 health checks with failover routing to a secondary Region, but during a recent primary Region outage, failover did not occur even though the primary was clearly unavailable. What is a likely cause?

choices.text: The secondary Region's resources were deployed in a different VPC than the primary's
The health check did not monitor the endpoint or path that was failing
The primary Region had more Availability Zones configured than the secondary Region
The DNS record's TTL was too low, preventing resolvers from caching the failover

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The health check must monitor the endpoint or path that actually failed. Otherwise it keeps reporting healthy and failover never triggers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Different VPC: doesn't affect DNS failover.
• AZ count: irrelevant.
• Low TTL: speeds failover rather than preventing it.

Key takeaway: health checks must reflect real failures.

stem: A team patches servers by SSH, and servers slowly drift apart. They want every change to be versioned, tested, and easy to roll back. Which practice fits BEST?

choices.text: Manual hotfixes recorded in a change log
Immutable infrastructure with pipeline-built AMIs
Snapshots of each server before every SSH change
Rolling in-place updates with a configuration management agent

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Immutable infrastructure bakes changes into a new, versioned image (for example, EC2 Image Builder) and replaces instances, so there's no drift, tests run on the exact image, and rollback means redeploying the previous image.

Why the other options are wrong:
• In-place updates: still mutate running servers, so drift can creep in.
• Manual hotfixes: the cause of the problem.
• Snapshots: help recovery, but changes are still manual and untested.

Key takeaway: never patch in place; replace with a new, versioned image.

stem: To ensure high availability, an Application Load Balancer's targets should be configured across which of the following?

choices.text: A single EC2 instance, for simplicity
Registered targets spread across multiple Availability Zones
On-premises servers exclusively, since ALB cannot target AWS resources
A single Availability Zone only, to minimize latency

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Targets registered across multiple AZs keep the application available if one AZ fails.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Single instance: single point of failure.
• On-premises only: ALB supports AWS targets.
• Single AZ: no AZ resilience.

Key takeaway: spread targets across AZs.

stem: Some targets behind an Application Load Balancer are being marked unhealthy and removed from rotation, reducing overall capacity during peak load, even though the application appears to be running normally. What should the architect check first?

choices.text: The target group health check path, interval, and thresholds
The Route 53 TTL settings for the application's domain name
The account's service quota for the number of VPCs per Region
The CloudFront cache behavior settings on the distribution

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Targets marked unhealthy while serving traffic point to health check settings: path, interval, timeout, and thresholds.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Route 53 TTL: unrelated.
• VPC quota: unrelated.
• CloudFront settings: unrelated to ALB health.

Key takeaway: check health check configuration first.

stem: A Lambda-based API opens many connections to Aurora. During failover, connections fail and the app returns errors for about 30 seconds. Which change reduces the impact MOST?

choices.text: Add more Aurora Replicas in the same AZ
Increase the Lambda timeout to 60 seconds
Enable Aurora Backtrack on the cluster
Disable Multi-AZ to avoid failovers
RDS Proxy between Lambda and Aurora

explanation:
Why this is correct:
RDS Proxy pools connections and keeps client connections open while it reconnects to the new writer, cutting perceived failover time and preventing connection storms from Lambda.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Longer Lambda timeout: requests wait longer but still fail on dropped connections.
• Backtrack: rewinds data; it's unrelated to failover.
• Replicas in one AZ: don't help connection handling and reduce AZ resilience.
• Disabling Multi-AZ: removes high availability.

Key takeaway: connection-heavy clients plus failover → RDS Proxy.

stem: A product launch in 3 weeks will need 4x the current EC2 vCPUs and Lambda concurrency. Which step prevents launch-day failures from quotas?

choices.text: Launch in a second Region on the day if the first one hits limits
Delete unused IAM roles to free up EC2 quota
Wait for AWS to raise quotas automatically when usage grows
Request Service Quotas increases now, with usage alarms

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Quota increases can take time, so request them ahead of known demand. Service Quotas integrates with CloudWatch usage metrics to alarm before limits are hit.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Automatic increases: most quotas don't rise on their own.
• Emergency second Region: complex and risky on launch day.
• Deleting IAM roles: unrelated to EC2 or Lambda quotas.

Key takeaway: plan quotas like capacity, before you need them.

stem: A team claims S3 Standard's '11 nines' means data is always accessible. An engineer disagrees. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: 11 nines applies only to S3 One Zone-IA
S3 Standard has 99.9% durability and 11 nines availability
11 nines is durability; Standard's availability design is 99.99%
11 nines covers both durability and availability for S3 Standard

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Durability is about not losing objects (99.999999999%). Availability is about being able to access them at a given moment, which S3 Standard designs for 99.99%. Data can be safe but briefly unavailable.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Both at 11 nines: conflates durability and availability.
• Reversed figures: durability is the 11-nines number.
• One Zone-IA: also designed for 11 nines durability but lower availability, and it's in one AZ.

Key takeaway: durability = won't lose it; availability = can reach it now.

stem: A company must retain a copy of critical S3 objects in a separate AWS Region to protect against a full Regional disaster, with new objects automatically copied as they are created. Which S3 feature should be enabled?

choices.text: S3 Object Lock
S3 Intelligent-Tiering
S3 Cross-Region Replication
S3 Transfer Acceleration

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cross-Region Replication copies new objects to a bucket in another Region automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Object Lock: retention.
• Intelligent-Tiering: cost.
• Transfer Acceleration: speed.

Key takeaway: Regional copies → CRR.

stem: A distributed application spans API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB, and the team needs to trace individual requests end-to-end to identify which component is causing intermittent latency. Which service should they use?

choices.text: AWS X-Ray
AWS Config
Amazon Inspector
Amazon CloudWatch Logs alone

explanation:
Why this is correct:
X-Ray traces requests across API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB to show where time is spent.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config: configuration.
• Inspector: vulnerabilities.
• Logs alone: no end-to-end request view.

Key takeaway: end-to-end request tracing → X-Ray.

stem: A three-tier application currently runs its web tier across multiple Availability Zones behind an ALB, but the entire database tier is a single RDS instance in one Availability Zone with no standby. Which single change would most directly eliminate the database as a single point of failure?

choices.text: Move the database to a larger instance class within the same Availability Zone
Increase the RDS instance's allocated storage size
Add more read replicas within the same Availability Zone as the primary
Enable a Multi-AZ deployment for the RDS instance

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Multi-AZ adds a synchronous standby in another AZ with automatic failover, removing the single-AZ database risk.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bigger instance: same AZ.
• More storage: no resilience.
• Replicas in the same AZ: same AZ risk.

Key takeaway: database AZ resilience → Multi-AZ.

stem: A financial services company runs a self-managed relational database on an EC2 instance that requires sustained 64,000 IOPS with sub-millisecond latency and 99.999% durability. Which EBS volume type should the solutions architect choose to meet this requirement?

choices.text: io2 Block Express
gp3
sc1
st1

explanation:
Why this is correct:
io2 Block Express provides sustained very high IOPS with sub-millisecond latency.

Why the other options are wrong:
• gp3: limited to 16,000 IOPS per volume.
• sc1 and st1: HDD.

Key takeaway: sustained high IOPS → io2 Block Express.

stem: Monthly reports are read a few times in the first 30 days, then rarely, but must open in milliseconds when requested. Objects average 50 MB. Which storage plan is MOST cost-effective?

choices.text: S3 One Zone-IA from day one for all reports
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 30 days
S3 Standard for the full retention period
Standard for 30 days, then S3 Standard-IA

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Standard-IA offers millisecond access at lower storage cost with a per-GB retrieval fee, which fits rarely read data that must still open instantly. Large objects avoid the IA minimum-size charge concern, and a 30-day lifecycle matches IA's minimum storage duration.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Glacier Flexible Retrieval: retrieval takes minutes to hours.
• Standard throughout: pays higher storage cost for rarely read data.
• One Zone-IA from day one: loses AZ resilience, and IA fees apply during the busy first month.

Key takeaway: rare but instant access → Standard-IA (or Glacier Instant Retrieval for rarer access).

stem: A company wants to extend on-premises storage to the cloud so that frequently accessed data is cached locally for low-latency access while the full data set is durably stored in Amazon S3, presented to on-premises applications as an iSCSI block device. Which AWS solution meets this requirement?

choices.text: Storage Gateway File Gateway
Storage Gateway Volume Gateway (cached)
Storage Gateway Tape Gateway
